findings.text: The applicant logs into TS-iPASS using the same credentials as the Consent to Establish (CTE) stage, and the data filed at CTE carries forward automatically into the Factory License application.

After incremental details are submitted and the fee paid online, document scrutiny is completed within 3 days, followed by a randomly assigned joint inspection team (applicant notified in advance by SMS), for a total of roughly 10 days to issuance.

The physical site inspection checks installed machinery and layout against the approved plan and verifies trial-production readiness where applicable; minor deviations are flagged for correction, but a major deviation requires a revised plan to be approved before the license can proceed.
Pending cases are taken up in the department's weekly case-by-case review meeting with the nodal commissioner, aimed at clearing cases proactively before they turn into delays.

The only step in an otherwise fully online process that still needs a physical presence is the site inspection itself; there is currently no remote or virtual inspection option, so the inspecting officer has to visit in person.

Nothing fresh is needed beyond what was already filed at the CTE stage, and the self-certification declaration filed at CTE is treated as covering Factory License compliance commitments too. The official also did not identify any duplication between state-level and central-level regulatory documentation for this service.

The license fee is auto-generated by the system based solely on installed power and number of workers, with no separate inspection fee; the amount also scales with the validity period chosen (1 to 5 years).
A revised or amended layout plan is called for only if the installed machinery ends up deviating from what was approved at the CTE stage.
Applicants can choose a validity period of 1 to 5 years at the time of application; in practice most opt for the full 5 years so they don't have to renew often.

Green-category units, and some orange-category units, get automatic renewal once the fee is paid with no fresh submission needed; the discussion did not go into how renewal differs for the remaining categories.

Deemed approval was not specifically confirmed for the Factory License in this discussion. In a related conversation on Consent to Establish, the same official confirmed TS-iPASS has a statutory deemed-approval provision, but noted it has never actually been triggered since approvals are consistently issued ahead of the deadline.

The official felt there is a reasonable case for formally extending the deemed-approval safeguard to the Factory License as well, though this was not directly confirmed for this specific service, and it would help to have it clarified and published.
Statutory registers and log books formerly required under factories law have largely been done away with or digitised, reducing paper-based record keeping after approval.
Ongoing compliance is overseen by the jurisdictional Inspector of Factories, whose name and contact details are displayed at the unit so workers know who to approach with grievances.

Risk-based (green/orange/red) classification feeds into both renewal and inspection; very-low-risk (green) units located in designated manufacturing zones can operate on a one-time, lifetime-valid acknowledgment instead of going through the full factory license process.

The mandatory in-person inspection, with no remote or digital verification option, can be burdensome because it depends on officer availability and scheduling — this applies even to green-category or otherwise low-risk premises.

Possible reform raised by the official: allow an optional remote/video verification route for low-risk (green-category) units, without diluting oversight for higher-risk categories — within the state's own discretion since this is a state procedural practice, not a Central Act mandate.
There is no fixed timeline for entrepreneurs to respond to scrutiny or inspection queries — intentionally so, to avoid pressuring applicants — but this can stretch case timelines unpredictably.

Possible reform: bring in an indicative, non-binding response window for entrepreneur query responses during inspection, to make timelines more predictable without removing the department's existing flexibility.

The amendment requirement triggered by a machinery/layout deviation stems from the Factories Act (a Central Act) and can't be removed without compromising safety oversight, but since it's a common and foreseeable scenario, it could potentially be fast-tracked as a defined sub-workflow rather than handled case by case.

The official described Telangana as the first state to bring in self-certification, a per-day monetary penalty on officers who delay applications, and a deemed-approval provision — all framed as accountability and reform measures.

Randomly assigned, SMS-notified joint inspections add transparency and cut down on discretion in how inspection teams are put together; a third-party certification option (registered agencies certifying factories, boilers, and pollution-related compliance) also takes some load off the department's own inspection capacity.

The official's overall sense was that the TS-iPASS single-window system for the Factory License is already quite streamlined, with limited room for further procedural reduction beyond the reforms noted.

Secondary research found a Telangana Factories Department circular (A1-6798-2015-EODB) citing a Factory License timeline of 7 days — confirming the ED's general order of magnitude, though not an exact match to the ED's ~10 days (3+7); the gap may reflect a different start point or a since-superseded 2015 figure.

Secondary research found validity-period sources that conflict with each other and with the ED: one cites 1/3/5-year options, another cites strictly annual renewal with an option to prepay, and a third cites a fixed calendar-year cycle. Automatic/deemed renewal was independently confirmed only for a different Telangana licence (Contract Labour), not specifically for the Factory License.

gaps.text: How renewal actually works for licence categories outside green and some-orange units (i.e., whether it requires fresh submission, inspection, or fee recalculation for the remaining categories) is not stated — the ED transcript explicitly notes 'the discussion didn't go into how renewal differs from the initial process' for these categories.

Deemed-approval status specifically for the Factory License (as opposed to the related Consent to Establish service) is not confirmed in the ED — neither the triggering timeline nor whether TS-iPASS Act 2014 Section 13's 'List of Deemed Approvals' schedule actually names Factory License as a scheduled service (secondary research could not retrieve that schedule to check).

The 'per-day monetary penalty on officers who delay applications,' cited by the official as a Telangana best practice, is never quantified anywhere in the ED transcript — no rupee amount or calculation basis is given.

Validity period: the ED states applicants can choose any term from 1 to 5 years, with green/some-orange units auto-renewing on fee payment. Secondary research found this contradicted across sources: one source describes only discrete 1/3/5-year options (not any year in between), another describes strictly annual renewal with a prepay option, and a third describes a fixed calendar-year validity cycle — no single secondary source corroborates the ED's exact framing.

Whether the TS-iPASS Act's Section 13 'List of Deemed Approvals' schedule actually names Factory License as a service covered by the statutory deemed-approval mechanism remains unresolved — secondary research could not retrieve the schedule itself to check, despite a government presentation referencing factories/boilers renewals generally as included under TS-iPASS.

The ED's ~10-day timeline (3 days scrutiny + 7 days inspection/issuance) is broadly corroborated by a Telangana Factories Department circular (A1-6798-2015-EODB) citing a 7-day Factory License timeline — confirming the same order of magnitude, even though the exact figure is not a 1:1 match (possibly a different start point or a since-superseded 2015 standard).

Telangana's full digital migration of CTE data to the Factory License application under a single TS-iPASS login (eliminating duplicate document submission), combined with randomly assigned SMS-notified joint inspections and weekly case-by-case review meetings with the nodal commissioner, stand out as practices worth other states replicating.
